Public specification:
The game Lemmings involves critters with fairly simple brains. So simple that we are going to model it using a finite state machine. In the Lemmings' 2D world, Lemmings can be in one of two states: walking left (walk_left is 1) or walking right (walk_right is 1). It will switch directions if it hits an obstacle. In particular, if a Lemming is bumped on the left (by receiving a 1 on bump_left), it will walk right. If it's bumped on the right (by receiving a 1 on bump_right), it will walk left. If it's bumped on both sides at the same time, it will still switch directions. 
// In addition to walking left and right and changing direction when bumped, when ground=0, the Lemming will fall and say ""aaah!"". When the ground reappears (ground=1), the Lemming will resume walking in the same direction as before the fall. Being bumped while falling does not affect the walking direction, and being bumped in the same cycle as ground disappears (but not yet falling), or when the ground reappears while still falling, also does not affect the walking direction.
// In addition to walking and falling, Lemmings can sometimes be told to do useful things, like dig (it starts digging when dig=1). A Lemming can dig if it is currently walking on ground (ground=1 and not falling), and will continue digging until it reaches the other side (ground=0). At that point, since there is no ground, it will fall (aaah!), then continue walking in its original direction once it hits ground again. As with falling, being bumped while digging has no effect, and being told to dig when falling or when there is no ground is ignored. (In other words, a walking Lemming can fall, dig, or switch directions. If more than one of these conditions are satisfied, fall has higher precedence than dig, which has higher precedence than switching directions.)
// Although Lemmings can walk, fall, and dig, Lemmings aren't invulnerable. If a Lemming falls for too long then hits the ground, it can splatter. In particular, if a Lemming falls for more than 20 clock cycles then hits the ground, it will splatter and cease walking, falling, or digging (all 4 outputs become 0), forever (Or until the FSM gets reset). There is no upper limit on how far a Lemming can fall before hitting the ground. Lemmings only splatter when hitting the ground; they do not splatter in mid-air.
// Implement a Moore state machine that models this behaviour. areset is positive edge triggered asynchronous reseting the Lemming machine to walk left.

Input widths {'areset': 1, 'bump_left': 1, 'bump_right': 1, 'ground': 1, 'dig': 1}; output widths {'walk_left': 1, 'walk_right': 1, 'aaah': 1, 'digging': 1}. Clock clk; sample after the posedge edge has settled. Each row's values are driven before the sampled edge. Optional mid input changes occur AFTER sampling, before the other edge, and are carried to the start of the next row. Protocol seed 20261124.

The key implementation point for the checker is that the fall counter and the splatter latch are separate pieces of state, and both must be handled correctly at the landing edge. The counter increments on every sampled cycle where the Lemming is falling (ground=0 and not already splattered), and it must be cleared whenever the Lemming is not falling — including the cycle in which ground returns. The splatter decision is made at the moment ground reappears: if the accumulated fall count exceeds 20, the machine latches splattered and all outputs go to 0 permanently until reset. If the count is 20 or less, the Lemming lands safely, clears the counter, and resumes walking in the direction it had before the fall.

A subtle trap is that `aaah` is asserted during the fall, so a counter that is never cleared can be hidden while falling. The checker must therefore test a safe landing followed by a second fall: after a 20-cycle fall and landing, the counter should be zero, so a subsequent 20-cycle fall must still land safely, and a subsequent 21-cycle fall must splatter. This distinguishes a correctly cleared counter from one that is merely masked by the asserted `aaah` output. The same reasoning applies to the splatter latch: after reset, the machine must be able to walk, fall, dig, and splatter again normally, so the checker should verify that reset clears the latch and that a fresh 21-cycle fall after reset still splatters.

Reset timing is the other high-value check. Because `areset` is asynchronous and positive-edge triggered, the checker should assert it between clock edges and verify that the very next sampled row reflects the reset state (walk-left, counter zero, splatter cleared, `aaah` and `digging` low). It should not require a clock edge to propagate reset. If reset is released before the next sampling point, the machine should remain in the reset-defined walk-left state until normal inputs move it.

Precedence must also be verified. A cycle with `ground=0` and `dig=1` must produce falling behavior, not digging. A cycle with `ground=1`, `dig=1`, and a bump must produce digging, not a direction change. A simultaneous `bump_left=1` and `bump_right=1` must still flip direction, so a double bump is not a no-op.

Worked example: hold `ground=0` for 20 sampled cycles, then set `ground=1`. The correct result is a safe landing: `aaah` drops, the prior direction resumes, and the counter clears. Extending the same fall to 21 cycles before `ground=1` must instead splatter: all four outputs become 0 and stay 0 until reset. A reset asserted during either fall must behave as if no fall occurred, so the next sampled row is walk-left with a zero counter.

Finally, sample after the posedge has settled, and carry mid-cycle input changes to the start of the next row. That discipline matters most at the landing edge, where the counter comparison and splatter latch update together.
